title: Decarboxylation for Infused Recipes | House of Zen
h1: Decarboxylation: The Step Every Infused Recipe Starts With
description: How to decarboxylate cannabis in a home oven: why heat matters, a common low-temperature starting point, and why homemade potency is never exact.
excerpt: Before flower goes into a recipe, it needs a slow stretch in a low oven. Here is what that step does, a common starting point and what you cannot know afterward.
pull: Your kitchen is not a lab, so homemade potency can never be known exactly.

blocks.html: Raw cannabis flower holds most of its THC in an acid form called THCA. Heat changes THCA into THC, and that change is called decarboxylation. A lighter or a vaporizer does it in a moment. Stirring raw flower into a batter does not do it reliably, which is why infused cooking usually begins with a separate step in the oven. Our piece on THC and THCA explains the chemistry a little further.
Think of it as toasting spices before they go into a dish. The heat stays low, and the kitchen will smell strongly of what you are making, so open a window and warn the household.

items: Flower from a licensed store, with its label kept for reference
A baking sheet lined with parchment, or an oven-safe dish with a lid, which holds in some of the smell
An oven thermometer, because home ovens often run hotter or cooler than their dials say
A timer, an airtight jar and something to label it with

sections.heading: A starting point in the oven

blocks.html: These numbers are common low-oven guidance, given here as a starting point rather than a rule. Ovens differ, and so does flower.

items: Break the flower into small pieces by hand. Keep it coarse, because powder is harder to strain later.
Spread it in a single layer and cover it loosely with foil, or close the dish.
Bake for 30 to 40 minutes, stirring gently once about halfway through. It should darken slightly, from green toward light brown.
Let it cool fully before you uncover it.
Move it to the airtight jar, label it with what it is and the date, and put it away from children.

blocks.html: Your kitchen is not a lab, so homemade potency can never be known exactly. The number on a flower label is itself a close estimate, and the oven, the timing and the recipe all change what ends up on your spoon.

That leaves two habits. Label everything you make and keep it away from children. And start low: try a small amount, wait at least two hours and only then decide whether you want more. Our piece on starting low goes into why.

Keep to the oven and to recipes based on fat. Do not make butane or alcohol extracts at home. Michigan’s adult-use law does not authorize separating plant resin with butane or any other substance whose flash point is below 100°F in a public place, a motor vehicle or at a home or on its immediate grounds, and high-proof drinking alcohol is such a substance. This is general information, not legal advice, as of October 2026.

Once your flower is ready, our recipe for simple infused honey is an easy first use. And if a kitchen project is more than you want, that is a perfectly good decision too, since our edibles come lab-tested and labeled. Ask our team, and we will gladly talk through either route with you.

faq.q: Do I have to decarboxylate before cooking with flower?
faq.a_html: For most infused recipes, yes. Without this step much of the THCA stays as it is, and the result is even harder to predict.

faq.q: Can I use a different temperature?
faq.a_html: Many cooks work somewhere between about 220 and 250°F and adjust the time to suit. Higher heat risks scorching the flower and driving off its aroma, so we would stay low.

faq.q: How strong will my batch be?
faq.a_html: Nobody can say exactly without a lab. Label it, keep it away from children and start low.
